# Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits {#sec-terminal}

If you mostly type prose, four things in this book may be new: keys that each program treats
differently, the symbols that code is full of, the paths that name files and folders, and the
keys and habits that make a terminal predictable, including how to read an error. Skip what you
already know. @sec-first-report is the place to practise all of it: almost everything in it is
typed by hand.

## The keyboard {#sec-keys-keyboard .unnumbered}

| Keys | What to know |
|---|---|
| **Shift**, **Caps Lock** | hold Shift for one capital letter, or for the upper symbol on a key; Caps Lock stays on until you press it again |
| **Backspace**, **Delete** | Backspace deletes to the left of the cursor, Delete to the right; on a Mac the key labelled Delete is Backspace, and Fn-Delete deletes to the right |
| **Enter** (Return) | starts a new line in a document, sends a message in a chat, and runs the command in a terminal |
| **Tab** | moves to the next field in a form and indents in an editor; in a terminal it completes names (below) |
| **Ctrl**, **Command** | a shortcut means holding the first key while you press the second: Ctrl+Z undoes on Windows and Linux, Command-Z on a Mac |

: Keys whose effect depends on the program you are in. Mac keys from Apple's "Mac keyboard shortcuts" page (checked 2026-11-16). {#tbl-keys-basic}

## Symbols this book uses {#sec-keys-symbols .unnumbered}

Code uses punctuation that prose rarely needs, and one wrong symbol stops a command. Each symbol
below appears in the book's prompts, commands or files.

| Symbol | Name | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| `` ` `` | backtick (grave accent) | around code in Markdown; three of them open a code block (@sec-md-code-fence) |
| `~` | tilde | your home folder in a path: `~/quarto-workshop` |
| `_` | underscore (Shift and the minus key) | file and column names: `_quarto.yml`, `water_coverage_total` |
| `-` | hyphen, also called dash or minus | options to a command: `quarto --version`; type the key itself, not a longer dash |
| `:` | colon | YAML settings, with a space after it: `title: "Visit London"` (@sec-yaml) |
| `'`, `"` | single and double quotes | keep words with spaces together: `cd "My Documents"`; text in Python and YAML |
| `&&` | double ampersand | runs a second command only if the first worked: `mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide` |
| `;` | semicolon | runs two commands on one terminal line, one after the other; rare in this book |
| `{ }` | braces, or curly brackets | executable cells such as `{python}`, and attributes such as `{.unnumbered}` |
| `( )` | parentheses, or round brackets | Python calls such as `len(df)`, and a Markdown link's address: `[text](url)` |
| `[ ]` | square brackets | a Markdown link's text, and Python lists: `["html", "pdf"]` |
| `/` | forward slash | between folders on a Mac, Linux and WSL, and in web addresses: `data/visits.csv` |
| `\` | backslash | between folders in Windows (`C:\Users`); at the end of a terminal line it continues the command on the next |
| `#` | hash | a Markdown heading, and a comment in Python, YAML and Bash scripts (not at a zsh prompt on a Mac, where it is passed to the command) |

: The symbols the book types most, and where each one appears. {#tbl-keys-symbols tbl-colwidths="[14,30,56]"}

::: pitfall
Two traps change a symbol without telling you. Word processors and notes apps turn straight quotes
into curly ones (“ ”) and two hyphens into a dash (—). A terminal and Python read those as different
characters, so a quoted name or an option such as `--version` stops working: copy prompts and
commands from the book or a plain-text editor. And some keyboard layouts make
symbols *dead keys*, which wait for the next key to accent it: Windows' United States-International
layout does this to `` ` ``, `'`, `"`, `~` and `^` (Microsoft's layout page, checked 2026-11-16),
and Spanish layouts to `` ` `` and `^`. Press Space after a dead key to get the symbol itself.
:::

## Terminal keys {#sec-keys-terminal .unnumbered}

A handful of keys make the terminal much faster and less error-prone. They are defaults in Bash, Ubuntu's
shell, and zsh, the Mac's, and in Windows Terminal and the Mac's Terminal app (GNU Bash and zsh line-editor
manuals; Microsoft and Apple keyboard documentation; all checked 2026-10-31).

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| **Enter** | runs the command you typed; press it once the whole command is there |
| **Space** | separates a command's parts, so put quotes round a name that contains one: `cd "My Documents"` |
| **Tab** | completes a file or command name; lists the choices when several match |
| **Up arrow**, **Down arrow** | step back and forward through earlier commands; edit one, then press Enter to run it |
| **Ctrl+C** | stops the running command (in Windows Terminal, copies instead when text is selected) |
| **Ctrl+Shift+C**, **Ctrl+Shift+V** | copy and paste in Windows Terminal and Ubuntu (Mac: Command-C, Command-V) |
| right-click | in Windows Terminal: copies a selection, or pastes when nothing is selected |

: Terminal keys worth knowing: running, completing, recalling, stopping, copying and pasting. {#tbl-terminal-keys}

::: pitfall
Ctrl+C in the agent's tab interrupts the agent, not a command. In Windows Terminal it copies only when
text is selected; with nothing selected it stops what is running.
:::

Other keys edit the line you are typing, clear the screen or find a command you typed before:

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+A**, **Ctrl+E** | jump to the start and the end of the line |
| **Ctrl+U** | delete to the start of the line (the whole line in zsh); **Ctrl+K** deletes to the end |
| **Ctrl+L** | clear the screen |
| **Ctrl+R** | search earlier commands as you type; Ctrl+R again for older matches, Enter runs it, Ctrl+G gives up |

: Terminal keys for editing the line, clearing the screen and searching earlier commands. {#tbl-terminal-line}

::: tryit
Open a second tab (Ctrl+Shift+D in Windows Terminal, Command-T on a Mac), type `ls ~/quarto-w` and press
**Tab**, then Enter. Press **Ctrl+L**, then **Ctrl+R** and type `ls`; then **Ctrl+A**, **Ctrl+E** and
**Ctrl+U**.

::: done
Ctrl+R found your `ls` command and Ctrl+U cleared it.
:::
:::

## Paths {#sec-keys-paths .unnumbered}

A *path* names a file or folder by the folders that lead to it, separated by `/`. An *absolute*
path starts at the top of the computer's folders, `/`, and means the same wherever you are:
`/home/ana/first-report` on Linux and WSL, `/Users/ana/first-report` on a Mac. A *relative*
path starts from the folder you are in: in `~/first-report`, `data/visits.csv` is the file
`visits.csv` in its `data` folder, and from your home folder the same path finds nothing.

| Path | Means |
|---|---|
| `~` | your home folder: `~/first-report` is the folder `first-report` inside it, from anywhere |
| `.` | the folder you are in: `open .` opens it on a Mac |
| `..` | the folder above: `cd ..` goes up one, and `../quarto-workshop` is a folder beside this one |
| `data/visits.csv` | relative: `visits.csv` in the `data` folder of the folder you are in |

: The short forms of paths that this book's commands use. {#tbl-keys-paths}

A "no such file" error often means a relative path read from the wrong folder: `pwd` says where
you are, and `ls` what is there.

A space separates a command's parts, so a name with a space reads as two names. Each shell says
so in its own words:

::: transcript
```text
$ mkdir "my reports"
$ cd my reports
bash: cd: too many arguments
```
:::

That is Bash on Ubuntu (5.2); zsh on a Mac answers `cd: string not in pwd: my`. Either way, keep
the name in one piece: put it in quotes, `cd "my reports"`, or put a backslash before the space,
`cd my\ reports`. Easiest of all, type `cd my` and press **Tab**: the shell completes the name and
types the backslash for you. Names you choose yourself are simpler without spaces:
`my-reports`.

## Reading an error {#sec-keys-errors .unnumbered}

A failed command often prints more than you need. Read it in this order.

**The first line.** It says what went wrong, usually after `ERROR:` or `error:`. Run
`uv run quarto render report.qmd` in the wrong folder and the line is:

::: transcript
```text
ERROR: No valid input files passed to render

Stack trace:
    at _Command.actionHandler (file:///Applications/quarto/bin/quarto.js:142967:11)
    ...
```
:::

Quarto found no `report.qmd` here: you are in the wrong folder, or the name is misspelt.

**Not the stack trace.** The lines after `Stack trace:`, each starting `at`, show where inside
Quarto the error surfaced. They are for Quarto's developers, not for you: skip them.

**The caret.** A mistake in a file's YAML ends with the lines around it, numbered, and a caret,
`^`, under the place where YAML gave up. Here `format: html` lost the space after its colon:

::: transcript
```text
ERROR: YAMLException: can not read a block mapping entry; a multiline key may not be an implicit key (4:1)

 1 |
 2 | title: "Five London Sights"
 3 | format:html
 4 |
-----^
```
:::

The numbers count lines from the opening `---`, which is line 1, and `(4:1)` means line 4,
character 1. YAML often notices a mistake one line *after* it, so look at the line the caret
points to and the line above: here the culprit is line 3.

When you ask for help, copy the whole thing all the same: the command and every line it printed,
stack trace included. The person or web chat helping you may need the part you skipped.
@sec-first-errors makes three common mistakes on purpose, and @sec-troubleshooting lists the
messages seen in practice, with their fixes.

## Habits {.unnumbered}

- **Know where you are.** Run `pwd` before starting an agent: its answer is the agent's root folder
  (@sec-root-folder).
- **Two tabs.** Keep the agent in one tab and commands such as `quarto preview` in another, both in the
  project folder.
- **New tab after installing.** A terminal learns where programs are when it starts, so a program installed
  a moment ago is "not found" until you open a new tab.
- **Read before you run.** Whether a command comes from the book, a web chat or the agent, read it before
  you press Enter or approve it, especially anything with `sudo` or `rm`.
- **Copy errors whole.** When something fails, copy the command and the entire error text; the useful line is
  rarely the last one.
- **Edit small files in the terminal.** `nano AGENTS.md` opens a file in a simple editor: **Ctrl+O**, then
  Enter, saves it, and **Ctrl+X** leaves. On a Mac, `nano` opens Pico, which uses the same keys (checked on
  macOS 26, 2026-11-12); both list their keys along the bottom of the screen.
